column4: The section defines the one in front against the one left behind; this ayah names exactly ٱلْمُسْتَقْدِمِينَ and ٱلْمُسْتَـْٔخِرِينَ, turning the herd's two positions into an all-encompassing divine knowledge.
This is the section's explicit Quranic herd scene: livestock are brought home in the evening and sent out in the morning, supplying both the foldward return and the day's departure to pasture.
The section's “first” and “last” are positions in one moving line; this ayah joins ٱلْأَوَّلِينَ and ٱلْـَٔاخِرِينَ before the next ayah gathers both groups together.
After 56:49 names the first and last, this ayah says that all are gathered at a known appointment; it gives the whole separated procession one final gathering place.
The keeper of a gathered company of birds inspects it and notices the missing hoopoe; this directly enacts the section's claim that the lost creature has an owner who knows it is gone.
The absent hoopoe of 27:20 returns after only a short absence and speaks to Solomon; it supplies the found creature's re-entry into the company.
Animals on earth and birds in flight are communities, and all are finally gathered to their Lord; the ayah combines flock, gathering, and the owner named as Rabb in the section.
The ayah places عَيْلَةً, need, beside God's promise يُغْنِكُمُ ٱللَّهُ, enriching you; it is the Quran's closest lexical expansion of the movement from عَآئِلًا to فَأَغْنَىٰ in the section.

Two orphan boys have a treasure preserved until maturity because their father was righteous; the father's absence and a good deliberately delayed until it can safely reach them concretize both dictionary claims about orphanhood.
Guardians test orphans until maturity and then deliver their property; this makes the section's “good that reaches the orphan late” a regulated delay ending in restitution.
Moses finds two women behind the other people, holding their flock back until the shepherds leave; وَوَجَدَ, the rear position, and the detained herd all meet in one scene.
Moses waters the lagging women's flock and then calls himself poor for whatever good his Lord sends; the scene joins aid reaching those held back with the needy searcher awaiting provision.
A people's sheep stray into a field by night and their owners' loss requires judgment; this is a concrete Quranic case of a flock crossing its proper boundary.
Moses identifies his staff by saying he uses it to beat down fodder for his sheep; it is the section's explicit Quranic meeting between the guiding staff and a tended flock.
God sends water and grows vegetation “in which you pasture” livestock; this supplies the pasture toward which the section's herd sets out at the beginning of the day.
The command to eat and pasture your livestock places human food and the herd's grazing within one provision; it makes the day's pasture a sign of the Provider.

Sacrificial camels stand in lines and are said to contain good for people; their ordered stance and فِيهَا خَيْرٌ meet the section's line of camels and its derivation of livestock from good and blessing.
God makes ships and livestock into mounts; the next ayah explicitly tells the rider to remember the Lord's blessing, joining the section's animal, rider, Rabb, and niʿma roots.
On settling upon the livestock mounts of 43:12, the rider remembers نِعْمَةَ رَبِّكُمْ; this directly reunites the herd-name's “blessing” sense with Rabb and riding.
Fine standing horses are displayed to Solomon in the evening; they form the equine company whose recall and necks appear in 38:33, matching two secondary details developed in the section.

Solomon orders the horses returned and strokes their legs and necks; “return them to me” enacts recalled animals, while ٱلْأَعْنَاقِ matches the section's designation of horses' necks as their foremost parts.
The birds are gathered, مَحْشُورَةً, and each is returning, أَوَّابٌ; this is a Quranic bird-company gathered back together, closely matching the dictionary scene for تأوّت الطير.
Abraham is told to call the birds and they will come swiftly; the ayah stages the section's secondary sense of calling dispersed animals so that they return to the caller's voice.
A person wanders bewildered on earth while companions call “come to us,” and the ayah identifies God's guidance as the true guidance; lostness, a directional call, and return meet exactly.
Moses and his servant forget their fish, which takes its way into the sea; this begins a literal lost-creature episode whose route must be recovered.
The servant recalls the fish at the rock and admits forgetting it while it took a remarkable route; the lost animal is connected to failed recollection and a now-identifiable location.
Moses says the lost fish's place is what they were seeking, and the two retrace their own footprints; this gives the section a precise Quranic scene of search ending by following a track backward.
Jacob sends his sons to search carefully for Joseph and his brother and forbids despair; the lost one's kin know whom they have lost and actively seek him, as the section says of the owner.
A caravan draws Joseph from the well and announces that it has found a boy, then hides him as merchandise; this is a found lost child whose true family ownership remains concealed.

Moses says knowledge is with his Lord in a record and that his Lord neither loses track nor forgets, لَا يَضِلُّ رَبِّى وَلَا يَنسَى; it is the decisive boundary on the image of an owner who cannot locate his animal.
The speakers say that what is before them, behind them, and between belongs to God, then add that the Lord is never forgetful; the line's positions and the unfailing Owner appear together.
Addressing the same prophetic companion as surah 93, the ayah says he has neither strayed nor erred; it gives the section's ضَالّ a direct later reassurance about the addressee.
The Israelites are condemned to wander bewildered through the land for forty years; this is the section's directionless condition expanded from one lost animal to an entire people.

God reminds a vulnerable, fearful group that He sheltered them, فَـَٔاوَىٰكُمْ, strengthened them, and provided good things; shelter and provision are the acts that bring the exposed back into safety.
The youths are told to take refuge in the cave, يَأْوِۦٓ إِلَى ٱلْكَهْفِ, where their Lord will spread mercy and prepare ease; the fold-like shelter is explicitly under Rabb's care.

Every creature's provision rests with God, who knows its dwelling and its place of deposit; this answers the image of an animal lost in an unknown waste with the Owner's complete knowledge and sustenance.

The ayah names the male and female of camels and cattle while rejecting invented sex-based prohibitions; that boundary illuminates the dictionary statement that the designation of a lost camel applies equally to male and female.
Ṣāliḥ calls the sign “God's she-camel” and commands his people to let her graze in God's land; animal, divine ownership, and released grazing are all explicit.
Ṣāliḥ again identifies God's she-camel and tells the people to leave her to feed in God's earth; it directly stages a female camel released to pasture while still belonging to a named owner.
One ewe stands against a flock of ninety-nine ewes whose owner seeks to absorb her into it; the isolated animal, the flock, and a contested claim of ownership make the herd's social boundary visible.
Wild beasts are gathered together; this is the Quran's compressed counterpart to the section's wild-animal leaders and the final collection of scattered animals.
The ayah says that both the latter and the former, ٱلْـَٔاخِرَةُ وَٱلْأُولَىٰ, belong to God; the front and rear of the section's line have one Owner.
God declares that both the Hereafter and the first life belong to Him; the two endpoints that the section pictures as herd positions are held within one ownership.
The warning addresses whoever chooses to advance or fall behind, يَتَقَدَّمَ أَوْ يَتَأَخَّرَ; the herd's opposed positions become a moral choice made within a single human company.
God says He created livestock for people and that they are their owners, لَهَا مَـٰلِكُونَ; the explicit ownership clarifies what is at stake when one animal becomes a ضالّة whose owner is unknown.
The command to give orphans their property and not consume it ensures that withheld good reaches the one for whom it was delayed.
The ayah addresses orphaned women to whom people do not give what is prescribed and commands justice for orphans; it exposes the human act that makes good arrive late.
The orphan's property may be approached only in the best way until maturity; the protective waiting period makes delay serve the orphan rather than the guardian.
The same boundary protects an orphan's property until maturity and couples it with fulfillment of covenants; delayed delivery remains an accountable trust.
The ayah calls setting orphans' affairs right “best” and makes them members of the believers' household; it answers delayed beneficence with repair and incorporation into a protecting group.
Feeding an orphaned relative on a day of hunger gives the section's slow-arriving good a concrete form and ties the exposed child back to kin.
The righteous feed an orphan, alongside the needy and captive, despite valuing the food; this is beneficence actually reaching the figure whose name the section derives from delayed good.
Pharaoh leads his people astray and does not guide them; he is the direct opposite of a hādī who occupies the front in order to bring those behind to the right place.
People who fail to understand and perceive are compared with livestock and called still more astray; it reverses the cared-for herd into a moral picture of creatures refusing guidance.
Those who do not hear or reason are like livestock and even further astray from the way; the herd here marks the boundary between being tended and being directionless.

God denies instituting the sāʾiba and related livestock taboos; the deliberately released animal from the section's dictionary is here bounded by a rejection of falsely attributing such release to God.
The rebuke “you do not honor the orphan” names the neglect that makes good late, directly opposing the shelter and care narrated and commanded in surah 93.
The denier violently repels the orphan; that expulsion from protection is the exact reversal of calling the vulnerable one back and giving shelter.
Those who consume orphans' wealth turn the good due to them into fire for themselves; the ayah exposes predation by the very people meant to safeguard delayed provision.
Noah's son says he will take refuge on a mountain, سَـَٔاوِىٓ, but is told there is no protector that day; it marks the limit of a shelter chosen apart from the true Owner's call.
The wrongdoers and their counterparts are ordered gathered; unlike the recovered herd's safe collection, this company is assembled for judgment and then directed toward Hell in 37:23.
The gathered wrongdoers of 37:22 are “guided” to the path of Hell; it is a grim reversal in which guidance and a common destination do not mean rescue.
People prefer the nearer life; beside the section's front/back reading of first and latter, this ayah makes preference for the first side of the pair the error explained in 87:17.
The Hereafter is better and more lasting, while 87:16 says people prefer the nearer life; the pair gives the first/last ordering a duration and value beyond spatial sequence.
People love the immediate life; this preference occupies the “first” end of the section's pair and is set against neglect of the Hereafter in 75:21.
People leave the Hereafter aside; with 75:20 it shows a procession morally disordered by attachment to what comes first.
For believers, gardens are نُزُلًا and جَنَّـٰتُ ٱلْمَأْوَىٰ; this is the welcoming final shelter contrasted with the fire-shelter of 32:20.
The defiantly disobedient have the Fire as their مَأْوَىٰ and are returned whenever they try to leave; the fold image becomes confinement rather than protective gathering.
For the one who prefers the nearer life, Hell is the مَأْوَىٰ; the familiar word for shelter is turned into the destination of a disordered preference.
For the one who fears the Lord and restrains desire, the Garden is the مَأْوَىٰ; paired with 79:39, it distinguishes the two ultimate gathering places.
Immediately before the foremost and lagging of 15:24, God says that He gives life, causes death, and remains the inheritor; the whole moving company passes while its Owner remains.
Immediately after God knows the foremost and lagging, the Lord gathers them all; it completes the ordered line as a company recovered into one assembly.
The livestock of 16:6 are first introduced as God's creation containing warmth, benefits, and food; it explains why the herd itself can bear the section's name of good and blessing.
After the herd's morning departure and evening return, livestock carry burdens to distant lands; this extends the ordered herd into a traveling train whose pace and rear matter.
Solomon is taught the speech of birds and recognizes what he has been given; that communicative bond makes his later notice of one missing bird and its answering report intelligible.
Solomon's hosts, including birds, are gathered and kept in ordered ranks; this is the section's moving line at the scale of a whole mixed company and sets up the missing hoopoe.
Solomon demands a clear explanation from the missing hoopoe; the keeper does not treat disappearance as ownerless but requires the absent member to account for its separation.
Between the display and recall of the horses, Solomon calls them a love of “the good” and mentions his Lord; the wording echoes the section's derivation of livestock from the good they contain.
Jacob turns away grieving for the still-lost Joseph until his eyes whiten; this gives the section's searching owner an affective human counterpart whose loss remains known across years.
Before Joseph physically returns, Jacob recognizes his scent from afar; the lost one is known by the one who loves him even while the surrounding family doubts.
The bearer brings Joseph's shirt and Jacob's sight returns; the long search reaches a bodily sign of reunion, completing the movement begun by the scent in 12:94.
Joseph draws his separated brother into his own lodging, ءَاوَىٰٓ إِلَيْهِ أَخَاهُ, and reveals their kinship; shelter here is reunion with the one who knows who the vulnerable arrival is.
Joseph receives his parents into his own protection and tells the family to enter Egypt safely; the root of shelter describes a scattered household gathered into security.
The youths take refuge in the cave and ask their Lord for mercy and right direction; the prayer joins shelter with guidance before 18:16 describes the refuge prepared for them.
Mary and Jesus are sheltered on a secure height with rest and flowing water; the root of مأوى here names a provisioned refuge for exposed dependents.
The Garden of مأوى stands by the lote tree of the boundary; it carries the section's ordinary animal shelter into the name of an ultimate abode.
A person's close clan is described as the family that shelters him, تُـْٔوِيهِ; the ayah preserves the social sense of being gathered into a protecting group even as judgment dissolves that loyalty.
God is named the First and the Last together; the section's two ends of a procession become coincident divine names rather than separated positions.
A person is told what he sent ahead and left behind, قَدَّمَ وَأَخَّرَ; the section's spatial front and rear shift into the temporal ordering of one's deeds.
Every soul learns what it sent ahead and left behind; this repeated secondary sense shows that the line's ordering can also describe consequences placed before or deferred.
The people around Medina are told not to remain behind God's messenger; it turns lagging behind a leader into failure to share the leader's arduous route.
God makes the prophets leaders who guide by His command; this states directly the relation implied by the dictionary's hādī as the foremost member of a company.
God appoints leaders who guide by His command when they are patient; leadership and guidance occupy the same forward position described in the section.
The ayah asks whether the one who guides to truth is more worthy to be followed than one needing guidance; it articulates the relation between the hādī at the front and those following.
Every people has a guide; the statement broadens the section's foremost hādī from an animal line into a human community's directional office.
The prayer asks God to make the faithful leaders for the God-conscious; it seeks the front position as responsibility for those who come behind.
As Moses sets toward Midian, he asks his Lord to guide him to the right way; the request supplies the directional uncertainty immediately resolved by finding the held-back flock in 28:23.
Pharaoh's forces pursue Moses' company at sunrise; the moving group at the beginning of day sets up the apparent loss of every route and the promise of guidance in 26:62.
With the pursuers behind and the sea ahead, Moses says his Lord is with him and will guide him; Rabb as owner-guide answers a whole company that seems to have nowhere to go.
People in the Fire say they obeyed their chiefs and great ones, who led them astray from the way; it is another failed front of the procession, where following produces loss.
At the trumpet blast, people leave their graves and hasten to their Lord; the Owner's signal summons a dispersed company back toward Him.
One cry suffices for everyone to be brought present before God; it gives the section's returning voice-call an eschatological completion.
The listener is told to await the day when the caller calls from a near place; the divine summons sets up the rapid emergence and gathering in 50:44.
The earth splits and people hasten out; God calls this an easy gathering, making the response to the caller a universal collection.
On the day God calls, people answer with praise and think they remained only briefly; the call brings the absent dead into responsive return.

When people's fathers are unknown, the community must call them brothers and allies rather than fabricate paternity; this sets a social boundary around the section's claim that human orphanhood is defined from the father's side.
Fear of injustice toward orphaned girls governs whom and how people may marry; the ayah makes the orphan's delayed or withheld due a test of justice in household formation.
True piety includes giving cherished wealth to orphans; it identifies the “good” that must cross the delay named by the section's orphan etymology.
When believers ask what to spend, orphans are named among the direct recipients; the answer maps beneficence toward the one for whom it otherwise comes slowly.
Israel's covenant couples worship of God with good conduct toward orphans; care is treated as a standing communal obligation, not an accidental kindness.
Worship of God is joined to doing good to parents, kin, and orphans; the ayah places the fatherless within the human circle charged to bring them good.
When orphans attend an estate division, they must receive provision and kind speech; the ayah prevents them from remaining at the rear of a distribution they witness.
Orphans receive a named share of spoils; communal wealth is routed to those whose good might otherwise be delayed.
Orphans receive a share of public wealth so that it does not circulate only among the rich; the distribution repairs the lag in provision structurally.
The livestock owned in 36:71 are subjected for people, some as mounts and some as food; ownership is expressed as care, use, and accountability for a tamed herd.
Livestock supply benefits and drinks and call for gratitude; this explains in Quranic terms why the section's herd-name belongs to the semantic family of blessing.
God makes livestock so that people ride some and eat some; the herd is presented as deliberately provided rather than abandoned in the wilderness.
Livestock carry people toward needs in their hearts, alongside ships; the animal company becomes a means by which a destination can be reached.
Livestock provide milk, many benefits, and food; the ayah makes the herd a sustained provision and supports the section's association of anʿām with good.
God brings out water and pasture from the earth; the next two ayat explicitly assign that pasture as provision to people and livestock.
The earth's water and pasture are provision for people and their livestock; the grazing scene is set within the Provider's preparation of the land.
The earth produces fruit and pasture; 80:32 identifies it as provision for people and livestock, giving the herd a prepared feeding ground.
The food and pasture are a provision for people and livestock; the animal line lives by a provision that precedes and awaits it.

The ayah joins eight livestock pairs with creation in mothers' wombs through layered stages; this gives Quranic form to the section's attention to animal sex and the maternal side of animal orphanhood.
